summary.text: A 23-year-old male healthcare professional developed erythematous and pruritic plaques in the right postauricular region about three weeks after continuous mask use during the COVID-19 pandemic. Examination showed erythematous scaly plaques extending from the retroauricular fold into the adjacent scalp and external auditory canal, consistent with early irritant contact dermatitis. He had no history of atopic dermatitis, psoriasis or seborrheic dermatitis, no new hair or skin products, and no systemic symptoms; psoriasis, allergic contact dermatitis and superficial fungal infection were considered and excluded, and laboratory evaluation was not indicated.

Topical betamethasone 0.05% cream gave temporary improvement within five days, but tapering to once every three days led to partial recurrence after two weeks. Tacrolimus 0.1% ointment and fusidic acid cream aggravated the lesions, and about 10 weeks from onset the picture had evolved into chronic seborrheic-type dermatitis with greasy scaling and crusting over the scalp; clinical findings indicated steroid dependence.

Management focused on discontinuing irritant products, gentle cleansing, fragrance-free emollients twice daily, short intermittent courses of low-potency topical corticosteroids, cautious corticosteroid withdrawal and patient education on mask hygiene, mask alternation and strap tension. Gradual improvement followed over the next weeks, with a partial response and residual erythema and scaling shown in Figure 3.
